ARTICLE
The Global Pact for the environment: a general instrument 
to face climate change
Domenico Amirante1
Published online: 16 May 2019 
© O.P. Jindal Global University (JGU) 2019
Abstract
Global Pact for the Environment emerged as an answer to the need for a general 
legal instrument on climate change which produces binding obligations. It is not just 
another international legal instrument which places legal obligations on state and 
non-state parties to address climate change. Rather, it is a novel instrument which 
links with national Constitutions and introduces innovative international legal prin-
ciples which bind state and non-state actors as well as multinational corporations in 
working together towards climate change. Also, the instrument moves beyond the 
polluter pays principle to focus on taking precautionary measures of maintaining as 
well as restoring the environment. Despite the criticism of the Pact being expressed 
by some scholars, the Global Pact presents itself as a promising document geared to 
address the pressing issue of climate change.
Keywords  Global Pact for the Environment · constitutionalization of environmental 
rights · principle of non-resilience
1  The struggle against climate change and the need for general legal 
instruments: the Global Pact for the environment
In recent years, climate change has been accelerating at an unprecedented and unex-
pected speed. Today, people all over the world in their daily lives are facing environ-
mental catastrophes, hurricanes, cyclones, floods and changes in the hydrogeologi-
cal structure of entire regions caused by climate change, with the risk of witnessing 
their native land being swallowed by the sea.1 This phenomenon was finally certified

by the Special Report of the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 
established by the UN), presented on 1 October, 2018 in Incheon, South Korea.2 
At that time, it was stated that if we want to save our planet, it will be necessary to 
reduce the emissions of greenhouse gases at a level below the already very ambi-
tious thresholds defined by the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement (COP 21) by modify-
ing the modalities of production, energy supply and, in short, our lifestyle. The prob-
lem is that due to the indecisiveness of several countries and also the withdrawal of 
some signatory states, the Paris Agreement to a great extent has remained a dead let-
ter to this day. The evidence of the difficulty in truthfully implementing this Treaty 
was confirmed by the meagre output of COP 24 held in in Katowice, Poland, in 
December 2018, where no real action was taken.
Considering the urgency of significant actions to face climate change, this sce-
nario demonstrates the failure of the current global environmental governance, 
claimed by several scholars.3 The urge for a change in global environmental gov-
ernance was finally certified by the UN Report, issued as recently as December 
2018, significantly titled “Gaps in international environmental law and environ-
ment-related instruments”.4 According to this Report, the “structure of international 
environmental governance is characterized by institutional fragmentation and 
a heterogeneous set of actors”5; this problem is exacerbated by a proliferation of 
environmental agreements with separate mandates that “ignore the unity, intercon-
nectedness and interdependence of the Earth’s ecosystem”, and “create potential for 
overlap and conflict, institutional and policy incoherence and increased financial and 
administrative burdens on states parties”.6 A panoply of economic and legal instru-
ments has been already created, set up and implemented to deal with the threat of 
climate change, both from the perspective of its reduction and of adaptation to it.7

However, if we want to “reimagine” climate change governance it is very important 
to start from a general reassessment of environmental law and policies, and, in legal 
terms, to general rules being capable of reorganizing the chaos of the multiplicity of 
different and often contradictory norms in this sector.
In other words, it is necessary that the international community in all its com-
ponents – international organizations, states, corporate firms and also citizens and 
organizations of civil society – make a decisive common effort to prevent national 
selfishness and the greed of international economic groups from definitively com-
promising the “basis of life” on earth. For these reasons, in 2016, an important ini-
tiative was launched by an international network of experts from around the world 
which comprised of the “Group of Experts for the Pact” (GEP), presided by Laurent 
Fabius, President of the French Constitutional Council and President of the COP 21, 
and coordinated by the Environment Committee of the Club des Juristes, a leading 
think tank in French society. The group of experts has drawn up, through a long 
drafting process, a Global Pact Plan, which brings together in a single international 
document the fundamental principles of environmental law and also proposes some 
innovative ones.
In just a few months, the Global Pact for the Environment gained considerable 
prominence in public opinion and in national and international political forums. The 
Pact was officially presented on June 24, 2017, at the University of the Sorbonne in 
Paris, by French President Emmanuel Macron in the presence, among others, of the 
former UN Secretary Ban Ki Moon, President Fabius of Constitutional Council and 
to dozens of lawyers from worldwide. On that occasion, the President of the French 
Republic pledged to present the draft of the pact to the General Assembly of the 
United Nations, thus fulfilling the commitment on September 19, 2017, in the mar-
gins of the ministerial week of the 72nd session of the General Assembly. Accord-
ing to the proponents, this new document, reiterating the will to actively engage in 
the fight against global warming, is the only valid instrument to address the issue of 
environmental protection at a global level in this particular historical and political 
moment.
On March 19, 2018, the European Commission also asked the Council for a man-
date to negotiate a global environmental pact in the name of the European Union. 
The request, in the form of a recommendation, followed the aforementioned initia-
tive presented by Macron in September 2017 at the United Nations General Assem-
bly in New York. The European Commission, with the Recommendation COM 
2018-138, aims to ensure that all EU Member states work together to ensure a high 
level of environmental protection. Finally, on ­10th May 2018, the United Nations 
General Assembly approved, with a resolution entitled “Towards a Global Pact 
for the Environment”, that marks the opening of international negotiations for the 
approval of the Pact.8 This is a great initial success, which could lead, for the first 
time, to the signature of a binding general and multilateral agreement for the protec-
tion of the environment. The Pact would reaffirm the responsibility of the interna-
tional community, and of the single states, involving them in actively working to

stop the planetary environmental disaster that is looming. The process for adopting 
the Pact was officially open in Nairobi at the beginning on 2019, with the first sub-
stantive session of the “Ad hoc Open-ended Working Group towards a Global Pact 
for the Environment”.9
Obviously, at present, there is neither an absolute certainty on the final approval 
of the Pact nor on the full transposition of its contents. However, this initiative has 
contributed to bringing environmental issues, and primarily climate change, back 
to the centre of the world political scene, in a phase in which the time factor is par-
ticularly important for all of us. In other words it has stressed that it is time for the 
international community to “take environment seriously”.10
2  The origins of the Global Pact for the Environment
Various international environmental instruments already exist in international law. 
Amongst them, the Stockholm Declaration 1972 and the Rio Declaration 1992 
have been iconic for recognition of some of the most shared principles of interna-
tional environmental law. Yet, considering the “soft” nature of international legal 
instruments provided for managing the environmental matter, the lack of a legal 
framework composed by enforceable obligations persists as a major problem. In 
fact, declarations usually expose a scope and a limit, avoiding a specific legal disci-
pline. In this legal framework, the Global Pact for the Environment intends to be an 
umbrella text which consolidate more than 500 international instruments, directly 
or indirectly related to the environment.11 But the sources of inspiration of the pact 
can also be traced back to several national Constitutions reflecting a growing con-
sensus on these principles. Among them the Charter of the Environment, in force 
since 2005 in France, represent a starting point, since it includes substantive rights 
and duties of individuals, which come together with procedural rights and public 
policy guidelines.12 The other international legal tool that lies at the heart of the 
Global Pact is the Paris Agreement 2015, which since its adoption, has reflected the

urgency felt by nations to reduce the anthropogenic greenhouse gas concentration 
in the atmosphere by a process that is fair, objective, active and tiered.13 The major 
strength of the Global Pact is that it will be enforceable, adding substance to all the 
promises assured by the Paris Agreement.
An interesting description of the nature and the role of the Global Pact is pointed 
out by Rene Cassin, Nobel Prize winner and one of the most important authors of 
the Pact, who imagines the Pact as a porch of a temple standing on four pillars: the 
first pillar represents personal rights and liberties, the second pillar represents the 
rights of individual vis-à-vis the community and in relation to the outside world, 
the third pillar represents the spiritual faculties, and the fourth pillar represents the 
economic, social and cultural rights. On the top of these columns, Cassin imagines 
a gable that binds individuals with the society.14 This image reproduces the mani-
fold essence and the plurality of fields in which the Global Pact would make effects, 
combining the legal framework with an international state-based demand to merge 
economic and environmental instances, as well as the community demand to care 
for the environment.
3  The relation of the Global Pact with national Constitutions
According to the introductory notes to the Global Pact for the Environment, it 
intends to be a fundamental tool for all the subjects involved in environmental gov-
ernance and to represent the “lowest common denominator” of many international, 
constitutional and legislative provisions already existing in most of the member 
countries of the international community. The Pact would, therefore, emerge as a 
conclusive element of a long legislative and constitutional evolution that, since the 
seventies of the last century, made environmental protection one of the crucial ele-
ments for the action of national governments. The Pact reflects this worldwide con-
stitutional evolution and is clearly inspired by it, as specified in the “White Paper” 
introducing it. For the authors of the Pact “the constitutionalisation of fundamental 
principles leads to the strengthening of their status in domestic law and the facilita-
tion of their implementation on a more global level, better than their embodiment in 
a specialized and sector-based approach”.15 Thus, the strain on environmental rights 
and principles contained in the Global Pact for the Environment, on the one hand, 
reflects and reinforces a growing consensus on these principles and, on the other 
hand, offers a means of guaranteeing their impact and effective implementation at 
the national level.
The Pact would also have a role in the most recent Constitutions, generating 
a new approach regarding the articulation of the relations between state and citi-
zens. However, the effect of this legally binding document will depend largely on

the social and legal approach of the countries. For this reason, some of them will 
need to integrate the principle of the Pact into their domestic laws.16 For example, 
in countries like the United States where there are no written constitutional norms 
on environment, the Global Pact for the Environment would be considered as non-
self-executing and would require domestic laws for its implementation. There is a 
similar situation also in other polluting-titans, such as China and Russia. Of course, 
the enforcement of the Pact can be reached also through judicial activism, as in the 
case of the Supreme Court of India, which held that customary international law can 
be implemented in India also in the absence of a specific legislation.17
Beyond this, we must consider that the issues related to legal aspects are not the 
only concern. In fact, sometimes soft laws find direct implementation, and on other 
occasions even binding treaties remain unimplemented due to strong disagreements 
about the substance and procedure laid down. Of course, the Pact cannot be merely 
reduced to soft law, since it establishes the rights of individuals to healthy environ-
ment and makes it imperative to implement this right through state norms. Rather, 
it needs to be adopted in the form of domestic laws and absorbed into national 
legal systems with laying down of specific procedure for making claims in cases of 
violations.
The Pact also involves important legal effects, requiring to states some specific 
performance through its newer principles, which prohibit degradation of environ-
ment and obliges restoration of eco-system rather than paying compensations. 
Hence, while absorbing the Pact into the domestic system, countries need to be care-
ful about the principles in the Pact they emphasize on. Since the Pact is an umbrella 
document, it provides for an assortment of principles, so that the principles intro-
duced in the national legislations will reflect the attitude of countries and the genu-
ineness of their concern for the environment.
4  Structure and contents of the Global Pact
The Global Pact is written in a direct style and based on a very simple structure. 
After the Preamble, there is the first part presenting general environmental rights 
and principles (Articles 1 to 8), while the second part contains some classical proce-
dural environmental principles (i.e. access to information, access to justice, etc., in 
Articles 9 to 13). The most innovative part is the third one (Articles 14 to 20), where 
new principles such as the non-regression or the resilience of environment are pro-
posed, along with the much needed principle defined as “diversity of national situa-
tions” (Article 20). The Pact then closes with some articles dedicated to monitoring, 
implementation and entry into force (Articles 21 to 26).
Article 1 of the Pact opens with a definition of the right to healthy environment, 
which provides that this right must guarantee not only full health and wellbeing, but

also “dignity, culture and the realization” of the person in a holistic vision in which, 
in addition to the protection of the “basis of life”, the right to the environment also 
refers to a more complex relational dimension between man, environment and terri-
tory.18 This article reflects the more recent evolution in environmental constitution-
alism considering the relation between man and environment at the core of the con-
stitutional system, and structuring the entire Constitution around this relation. For 
example, the new Constitutions of Ecuador (2008) and Bolivia (2009), represent, for 
many scholars, a “transition from a juridical anthropocentric orientation of rights to 
an eco-centric one”.19
Another particularly important emphasis concerns the “environmental duties” for 
the first time contained in an international document. As far as international duties 
on environmental matters are concerned, Article 2 expects that “Every state or inter-
national institution, every person, physical or legal, public or private, has a duty to 
protect the environment”. To this end, everyone contributes, at their own levels to 
the conservation, protection and restoration of the integrity of the Earth’s ecosys-
tem”. It is important to note that the Pact refers not only to states, but also to people 
and to the civil society, directly concerning individuals and collective groups. The 
accent on the role of non-state actors and civil society, is another important bench-
mark of the Global Pact, stressed in the Preamble (“welcoming the vital role of non-
state actors, including civil society, economic actors”) and then openly highlighted 
in Article 14. This article entitled as “role of non-state actors and subnational enti-
ties”, clearly emphasizes that “the Parties shall take the necessary measures to 
encourage the implementation of this Pact by non-state actors and subnational enti-
ties, including civil society, economic actors, cities and regions taking into account 
their vital role in the protection of the environment”.
The Global Pact then delineates the fundamental principles for the protection 
of the environment from Article 3 until Article 20. It starts from the most consoli-
dated ones, constituting the main axis of environmental protection in recent decades, 
to some particularly innovative ones, among which, in particular, the principle of 
“non-regression of the environment” stands out.
Thus, the list of fundamental provisions enshrined by the Global Pact starts with 
general principles, such as those of integration and sustainable development and 
intergenerational equity (Article 3 and 4), to reproduce the “triad” of management 
principles of the environment commonly defined as: “polluters pays”, “prevention” 
and “precautionary” (Articles 5 to 8), which represent the backbone of the entire 
environmental protection system. The three principles are placed in an evolutionary 
path linked to the emergence of different epistemological models regarding the rela-
tionship between law and the environment, and form a system that assumes a pre-
scriptive and structuring value towards the actions undertaken in the environmental

field. This system is based on the centrality of the principle of prevention, under-
stood as an ordinary modality of the action in the environmental field and which 
must therefore inform all the moments of public action, but, in present days, also of 
private action. Therefore, the other two principles perform both auxiliary and inte-
grative functions with regard to prevention. For example, the “polluter pays” princi-
ple represents not only an instrument for integrating prevention objectives into eco-
nomic activities and public and social policies (e.g. the so called “internalization” of 
environmental costs), but also a standard to be used in cases of “failure of preven-
tion”, which, unfortunately, do not appear to be negligible at present.
The precautionary principle acts instead “upstream” and it is usually called upon 
to intervene in cases where the preventive approach cannot be applied. It is essen-
tially based on the lack of faith in objective science on the part of law and politics. 
In this case, the law declares the incapacity of science to supply solutions to all envi-
ronmental problems, and the consequent insufficiency of curative and preventive 
models. Here, the precautionary principle plays an active role, requiring the public 
actors, faced with situations of necessity, to make choices in any event, even when 
not supported by scientific accuracy. In my opinion, “this is one of the characterizing 
elements of the precautionary principle: the expansion of political and administra-
tive discretion with regards to choices having a technical and scientific content. The 
precautionary principle brings out the change of legitimization between science and 
politics, placing the responsible political and administrative parties at the forefront 
of difficult decisions”.20 In other words, this principle is the expression of a new 
institutional philosophy that is equipped to cope with uncertain or potential risks.
The Global Pact also specifies a series of procedural principles from Articles 9 
through 13, namely on access to environmental information, public participation, 
and on access to justice, education and training, research and innovation. Then, it 
enunciates a series of innovative principles of great importance in the Articles 14 to 
20. After the already mentioned principle concerning the “role of non-state actors 
and subnational entities” (Article 14), these innovative principles extend from the 
affirmation of the role of the effectiveness of environmental norms (Article 15) and 
the newest principles of resilience and non-regression (Articles 16 to17, which will 
be described in the next paragraph of this paper), to conclude with a series of princi-
ples primarily aimed to define the “environmental relations” between states. Among 
the latter, must be noted the “diversity of national situations” principle (Article 20), 
according to which “the special situation and needs of developing countries, particu-
larly the least developed and those most environmentally vulnerable, shall be given 
special attention”. This principle represents a further evolution of the “common but 
differentiated responsibilities” formula in terms of environmental protection. It is 
aimed at pursuing compensatory effects for those countries historically damaged by 
the disorderly and predatory growth of the main industrialized countries. Article 20

The Pact then concludes with a series of rules concerning the signing procedures,

5  New principles in the Global Pact
The greatest merit of the Global Pact is grouping environmental law rights and prin-
ciples in a single document and giving them binding force. If this is true for the 
right to healthy environment declaimed in a holistic perspective (Article 1), it is 
even more relevant for the already mentioned “triad” of the principles concerning 
the “management” of environment. But the real innovation of the Global Pact con-
sists in the introduction of the “non-regression” principle, affirmed by Article 17. 
The non-regression principle states that “the Parties and their sub-national entities 
refrain from allowing activities or adopting norms that have the effect of reducing 
the global level of environmental protection guaranteed by current law”. In other 
words, this principle intends to prevent public authorities from making laws which 
adversely affect the environment. As pointed out by the renowned environmental 
scholar Michel Prieur22 known as the academic “father” of this principle, non-
regression is addressed to legislators and administrative bodies and is also a guide 
for judicial interpretation. For Prieur, environmental regression takes many forms: 
but “it is seldom explicit, since governments do not have the courage to announce 
backtracking in environmental protection officially for fear of an unfavourable public 
response from environmental and consumer NGOs”.23 For this reason, “faced with 
this diversity of forms of regression, environmental lawyers must respond firmly and 
rely on implacable legal arguments” .24
According to Kenig-Witkowska the non-regression principles include both “the 
prohibition of the adoption of either new regulation in order to reduce the level of 
protection or ones which would be more favourable for the environment”.25 F. Hau-
mont, considering the long date experience of the application of this principle in 
Belgium, asserts that non-regression has an undeniable effect on the methodology 
used for drafting new laws and regulations. Referring to Belgium, Haumont high-
lights that “the legislative and executive authorities in their regulatory functions 
know that compliance with the principle of non-regression will be monitored a pri-
ori by the Legislative Division of the Council of State and a posteriori in the context 
of constitutional or administrative disputes … the legislator (in the broadest sense)

The principle of resilience mentioned in Article 16 completes and integrates the 
non-regression requiring that “the Parties shall take necessary measures to main-
tain and restore the diversity and capacity of ecosystems and human communities to 
withstand environmental disrup- tions and degradation and to recover and adapt.”. 
According to Kenig-Witkowska, the principle can be referred back to the concept of 
“improvement” of the environment laid down in the Stockholm Declaration (Princi-
ple 1) or to the spirit of the 1982 World Charter for Nature. For this author, this prin-
ciple means that “the purpose of environmental policy must be not only to remedy 
environmental damage but also to strengthen the capacity of ecosystems to recover 
and achieve equilibrium in the functioning of ecosystems”.27
6  Conclusion: the Global Pact for the environment, an open debate
Generally speaking the Pact has been welcomed and even strongly supported by 
most jurists and institutions, but it has also opened an interesting debate between the 
supporters of a robust recognition of the centrality of environmental protection in 
the legal order (at the international and constitutional levels) and those who are still 
sceptical about an international “juridification” of environmental protection through 
a general international binding document.
For Parejo Navajas and Lobel “the Global Pact, and the enforceable right to a 
healthy environment that it intends to codify, would be a milestone achievement in 
the fight for environmental protection” and a fundamental tool to fight against cli-
mate change.28 In the same direction Zlatescu asserts that the Global Pact “would 
provide a text of general applicability that would lead to the coordination of norms 
and institutions in international environmental law” and it “would codify the princi-
ples stated in the agreements so far, establishing legal rights and responsibilities that 
can be invoked in national and international courts”.29

criticism to the Pact: firstly concerning the diplomatic and symbolic relevance of the 
Pact (and its level of contribution to global environmental law and governance) and, 
secondly, its potential at the operational level, both of international environmental 
law and of global environmental governance.30 The authors claim that the Pact is 
very similar to the IUCN Draft Covenant (adopted in 1994),31 being an umbrella 
document on international environmental principles. For them, the binding value of 
a document alone does not improve environmental quality and effectiveness of inter-
national environmental law, as it does not directly address the roots of inadequate 
environmental protection.32
Notwithstanding the interest of such criticism, the comparison between the 
Global Pact and the IUCN Draft Covenant on Environment and Development 
appears relatively narrow, according to two important perspectives: comparative 
methodology and understanding aims and effectiveness of the Global Pact. About 
the first point (the comparison between these two documents) it has to be noted that 
the IUCN Draft Covenant tries to consolidate and develop already existing envi-
ronmental and developmental principles in a pure legal framework, which remains 
complex to understand and interpret without a technical background. The nature of 
these two documents is clearly different, as well as their aims: on one side, there is 
a 238 pages long text composed of 83 Articles grouped in 11 sections, on the other, 
there are 26 Articles providing a general framework or an evolving milieu for start-
ing a global enforcement of environmental provisions.
Regarding the goals and the effectiveness of both documents, some remarks must 
be noted. As previously stated, legal and technical details are, of course, necessary 
and welcomed for providing a framework to the environmental discipline, but such 
kind of documents, despite their attitude, cannot be directly addressed to civil soci-
ety and to individuals, and require intermediate hermeneutical activities by experts. 
On the contrary, the Global Pact for the Environment tries to create a general and 
coherent framework without falling into a merely legalistic perspective. It should be 
noted, in fact, that a strictly binding document would not have easily been accepted, 
discussed and signed by parties, especially by some states reluctant to limit them-
selves in such cases (the US contemporary environmental policy is a proper example 
and does not need supplementary explanations). According to these assumptions, 
it should be noted that the framers of the Global Pact for the Environment learned 
the lesson provided by the IUCN Draft Covenant: to become enforceable it must be 
accessible to the large public without sacrificing accuracy.

Kotzé and French also lamented that the Pact is not very human-rights centric.33 
On this matter, without denying that human rights and environment are intrinsically 
connected, we think that the institutional philosophy underlying the Pact tries to 
strike a balance between the recognition of rights and the enumeration of “rules of 
conduct” for all the subjects involved in environmental issues, including states and 
the private corporations. This reflects also the mixed common law/civil law compo-
sition of the Group of experts that drafted the document, a very important feature of 
the Pact that is not always reflected in the documents produced at the international 
level.
A different kind of criticism to the Pact is addressed by Susan Biniaz, cautioning 
that the existing equilibrium in the field of international environmental law may get 
disbalanced by the “juridification” of some principles in the Global Pact.34 Biniaz 
warns that normative principles such as the precautionary ones are better left “non-
binding”; adding them to the Global Pact may lead to excessively homogenising 
international environmental law, which, on the contrary, is extremely region-specific 
in nature. Against this thesis, it is sufficient to note that a vast majority of environ-
mental jurists believe that combination of human rights with environmental prin-
ciples is “the need of the hour”, and that the Global Pact exactly integrates human 
rights and environmental management principles in a coherent environmental law 
framework.
On the whole, we can conclude that the Global Pact is a document in which inno-
vation and courage go hand in hand with the pursuit of an international consensus 
and the rigor in the formulation of the principles. Showing a realistic concern on 
international balances, the Global Pact has the ambition to represent an inescapable 
point of reference for the future generations of lawyers, legislators and policy-mak-
ers, as well as for economic actors and the civil society.
